sourceUnits.label: Listening comprehension activities (A1–A2)
sourceUnits.locator: CEFR 2001 ch. 4 · aural reception (section number not verified this round)
sourceUnits.rationale: PCIC A1-A2 inventories list genres to be received or produced and learning procedures, but do not list this category as such; it is part of CEFR communicative language activities and is needed to run a course. PCIC Géneros marks oral genres for reception (R) but sets no listening tasks or task conditions.

sourceUnits.label: Sustained spoken production: short monologues (A1–A2)
sourceUnits.locator: CEFR 2001 ch. 4 · oral production (section number not verified this round)
sourceUnits.rationale: PCIC A1-A2 inventories list genres to be received or produced and learning procedures, but do not list this category as such; it is part of CEFR communicative language activities and is needed to run a course. PCIC Géneros A1-A2 lists presentaciones públicas for reception only; prepared self-presentations are a standard A1–A2 production task.

sourceUnits.label: Mediation: relaying simple information between languages (A1–A2)
sourceUnits.locator: CEFR Companion Volume 2020 · mediation (not obtained this round)
sourceUnits.rationale: PCIC A1-A2 inventories list genres to be received or produced and learning procedures, but do not list this category as such; it is part of CEFR communicative language activities and is needed to run a course. PCIC covers intercultural mediation (Habilidades y actitudes 4) but not linguistic mediation such as relaying a sign or a short message to someone who does not speak Spanish.

sourceUnits.label: Cognates and false friends for English-speaking learners
sourceUnits.locator: Editorial (L1-specific); no framework locator
sourceUnits.rationale: PCIC inventories are written for all learners and do not address a particular first language. English-speaking learners can exploit thousands of Latin-based cognates and need warning about a small set of frequent false friends; the course is written for English speakers (instructionLang en).

units.title: Letters, sounds and first greetings
units.goal: Can spell their own name aloud, greet and say goodbye at the right time of day, thank, apologise, and ask someone to repeat or slow down
units.rationale: Entry point: real exchanges that need no grammar. The five vowels and letter names are the base for reading every later word aloud.

units.title: Who I am: name, origin and how to address people
units.goal: Can say and ask name, nationality and where someone is from, introduce someone, and choose tú or usted
units.rationale: Identity is the most frequent first conversation; ser and subject pronouns are the first sentence skeleton. Reading words aloud from spelling comes now so every later word can be read.

units.title: Numbers, age and contact details
units.goal: Can ask and give age, phone number, address and email, and fill these into a form after hearing them
units.rationale: Personal data exchanges need numbers, tener and question words; together they unlock the first information-gap tasks.

units.title: Things and people around me
units.goal: Can name and describe classroom objects and everyday things with the right article, gender and agreement, and point to them with este/ese/aquel
units.rationale: Gender and agreement touch every noun phrase from now on, so they come right after the first sentences; classroom language lets the course run in Spanish.

units.title: Family and possessions
units.goal: Can talk about their family, say whose things are and describe people's appearance and character simply
units.rationale: Possessives and de build on articles and agreement; family is the next most frequent topic after identity.

units.title: My day: regular verbs, time and dates
units.goal: Can describe their weekday routine with times, say what day and date it is, ask yes/no questions and say what they are doing later today
units.rationale: The regular present is the workhorse tense; it comes once nouns and pronouns are in place. Clock time and dates attach naturally to routines.

units.title: Where things are: places, home and weather
units.goal: Can say what there is in a place, where things and places are, describe their home and town, and talk about the weather
units.rationale: hay and estar are the two ways of locating things; contrasting them early prevents a persistent error. Home, town and weather give the material.

units.title: Likes, free time and agreeing
units.goal: Can say what they like and don't like, how much, react with también/tampoco, and say which of two options they prefer
units.rationale: gustar reverses the English subject/object pattern and is the most persistent A1 error, so it gets its own unit with plenty of free-time vocabulary to practise on.

units.title: Eating out and saying yes or no
units.goal: Can order food and drinks, say what they want, accept or decline offers politely, and know when Spanish speakers eat
units.rationale: Ordering is the first high-stakes transaction; quiero and polite yes/no answers build directly on gustar and articles.

units.title: Shopping and prices
units.goal: Can ask for products, sizes and prices, understand prices and large numbers, and complete a simple purchase
units.rationale: Shopping recycles numbers, colours and demonstratives in a transaction with a clear outcome.

units.title: Getting around town
units.goal: Can say where they are going and how, ask for and follow simple directions, and talk about transport and travel
units.rationale: ir and movement verbs plus ordinals and place expressions make directions possible; travel is a core need for adult learners.

units.title: What I know, can do and think
units.goal: Can say what they know and can do, give a simple opinion with creo que, evaluate things as good or bad, say something is possible, and show they are listening
units.rationale: Opinions and evaluations need only ser + adjective and creo que + clause, which are now available; saber/conocer is a classic split for English speakers.

units.title: Reasons, purposes and which one
units.goal: Can explain why they do things and what for, identify people and things with que-clauses, and use infinitives after verbs
units.rationale: Porque, para + infinitive and que-relatives turn single sentences into the first linked explanations needed for short texts.

units.title: Reading and writing short texts
units.goal: Can read signs, timetables, menus and simple forms, write short messages and postcards, and write a short description of a person, object or place with correct spelling and punctuation
units.rationale: Closes A1 by turning the grammar and vocabulary into text: written accent rules and punctuation now have enough words to practise on.

units.title: Everyday verbs: stem changes and irregular yo forms
units.goal: Can talk about habits and how often they do things using the most frequent irregular present-tense verbs, and talk about work and studies
units.rationale: A2 opens by completing the present tense: the most frequent verbs (querer, poder, tener, hacer, salir) are irregular, and A1 used them only as chunks.

units.title: How I feel: estar, states and the body
units.goal: Can say how they and others feel, describe physical sensations and pain, choose ser or estar with adjectives, and explain a health problem simply
units.rationale: estar + adjective completes the ser/estar picture begun at A1; feelings and body vocabulary give immediate personal use.

units.title: Plans, wishes and invitations
units.goal: Can talk about future plans and intentions, say what they would like to do, and make, accept and turn down invitations and suggestions
units.rationale: ir a + infinitive needs only ir (A1) and the infinitive; invitations combine it with the softened refusals that A2 functions require.

units.title: Obligation, permission and favours
units.goal: Can say what is necessary or not, ask for and give permission, ask favours and help, and give simple advice and warnings
units.rationale: tener que and hay que build on tener and infinitives; poder (now that stem changes are known) carries permission, ability and polite requests.

units.title: Instructions and directions
units.goal: Can give and follow instructions and step-by-step directions, attract someone's attention appropriately, and use llevar/traer correctly
units.rationale: Affirmative imperatives need the stem-changing and irregular presents from a2-01; directions and recipes are their natural context.

units.title: Him, her, it, them: object pronouns
units.goal: Can avoid repeating nouns by using direct and indirect object pronouns in the right position, and talk about what interests or delights them
units.rationale: Object pronouns are needed for natural replies (¿Tienes el billete? – Sí, lo tengo) and for gustar-type verbs beyond gustar; they come after imperatives and periphrases so that attachment can be practised in both positions.

units.title: What I have done: experiences and the recent past
units.goal: Can talk about experiences in their life and what they have done today or this week, and say what has or hasn't happened yet
units.rationale: The present perfect is the first past tense: regular participles plus haber, and it connects to the present (hoy, esta semana) — the most frequent past in Peninsular speech for today's events.

units.title: What happened: the preterite
units.goal: Can say what they did at a specific time in the past, including weekends, trips and biographies, using frequent regular and irregular verbs
units.rationale: The preterite follows the perfect: learners already have a past for experiences and today; now they add completed events at a finished time, which the contrast KC makes explicit.

units.title: How things were: the imperfect and simple narratives
units.goal: Can describe how things used to be and the background to past events, and tell a simple story or anecdote in order
units.rationale: The imperfect is added after the preterite so that narrative can combine background (imperfect) and events (preterite); connectors make the story readable.

units.title: Describing and comparing things
units.goal: Can describe objects, places and people in more detail, compare them, react with exclamations, and say whose something is with stressed possessives
units.rationale: Shopping, housing and travel at A2 all require choosing between options; comparison and richer description reuse ser/estar and agreement from earlier units.

units.title: How much, nobody and nothing: quantity, negation and articles
units.goal: Can talk about quantities and existence with indefinite words (alguien, nada, todos, demasiado), make negative statements with double negation, and use or omit articles naturally
units.rationale: These closed-class words cause many A2 errors; grouping them lets learners compare positive and negative pairs (algo/nada, alguien/nadie) and article presence/absence in one place.

units.title: What is happening now and when things happen
units.goal: Can describe actions in progress, link events in time with cuando / antes de / después de, say how long something has been going on, and ask a wider range of questions
units.rationale: estar + gerund and time clauses complete the time toolkit after past tenses; the extended question words support the interaction activities that follow.

units.title: Opinions, conditions and reasons
units.goal: Can agree and disagree, say how sure they are, give reasons and consequences, state simple real conditions with si, and say what they remember or have forgotten
units.rationale: Discussion functions at A2 require linking ideas (si, por eso, porque) and graded certainty; por and para are introduced here as cause vs purpose.

units.title: On the phone and in conversation
units.goal: Can make and take simple phone calls, keep a conversation going by referring back without repeating, and follow everyday conversations and announcements
units.rationale: Phone calls remove visual support and need the pronouns and attention-getters of earlier units; conversation management ties A2 grammar into longer exchanges.

units.title: Social life, celebrations and texts
units.goal: Can welcome people, congratulate and wish well, write short letters, emails and descriptions, read short everyday texts, relay simple information for someone who doesn't speak Spanish, and reflect on cultural differences
units.rationale: Writing and reading activities at A2 integrate the grammar of the level; social rituals and intercultural reflection close the level before topic vocabulary.

units.title: The wider world: services, media, nature and culture
units.goal: Can handle vocabulary for money and public services, media and technology, nature and geography, and name a few cultural references from the Spanish-speaking world
units.rationale: These topic areas close A2 because they rely on the grammar of the level (past tenses for history and news, comparison for geography) and broaden learners' world beyond the personal domain.

tracks.title: Children 8–12 (already reading and writing in their first language)
tracks.learner: Children aged 8–12 who read and write confidently in English (or another first language); 2–3 lessons a week of 40–50 minutes; school or after-school setting
tracks.goal: Reach a solid A1 and a partial A2: talk about themselves, family, school, likes and daily life, tell what they did, and read and write short texts
tracks.entry: Start from sounds, letters and greetings (no grammar needed), then build vocabulary around the child's own world before verbs; songs, games and pictures carry the grammar as chunks first
tracks.adapt: Little grammar terminology; mastery checks favour match, listen-comprehend, role-play and short written production. Adult topics (work, money, politics, formal emails, telephone services) and abstract A2 items (certainty scales, por/para, perfect vs preterite variation, mediation) are left out; they can be added when the learner moves on. Tú forms dominate; usted is recognised.

stages.title: ¡Hola! Sounds, letters and me
My things, my family, my house
My day, food and what I like
Out and about; reading and writing
Feelings, plans and rules
Telling what happened
Comparing, animals and the world

tracks.title: Teenagers and students (school or university course, exam-oriented)
tracks.learner: Learners aged 13–22 in a school or university Spanish course, comfortable with grammar explanations; 3–4 hours a week; may sit DELE A1/A2 or a school exam
tracks.goal: Complete A1 and A2 with full coverage of the grammar and functions, ready for an A2 exam (reading, listening, writing an email, speaking interaction)
tracks.entry: Same no-grammar entry as the main path, but moves quickly into the classroom and personal-information units because students need to function in a Spanish-taught class
tracks.adapt: Covers every KC. Past tenses are moved forward in A2 (after plans) because exams and narratives depend on them; rules, imperatives and comparison follow. Mastery checks include exam-like item types (read-comprehend, listen-comprehend, situated-production-written). Teachers should state which variety of perfect/preterite use the exam expects.

stages.title: First contact and classroom survival
Me, my family and my routine
Going out, opinions and short texts
Irregular verbs, feelings and plans
Past tenses and stories (exam core)
Rules, instructions, comparing and arguing
Exam tasks: conversation, emails, texts and culture

tracks.title: Adults: everyday life and travel
tracks.learner: Adults with limited time (1–3 hours a week) who want to travel, live temporarily or socialise in a Spanish-speaking country; prefer practical phrases over grammar study
tracks.goal: Handle travel and everyday transactions early (ordering, buying, getting around), then talk about themselves and their experiences and solve common problems (health, phone, services)
tracks.entry: Starts with greetings and the survival units (food, shopping, transport) so that learners can use Spanish on a trip within weeks; prerequisites such as numbers and articles are pulled in automatically
tracks.adapt: Usted and tú both practised from the start; the learner's target region decides vocabulary (móvil/celular, coger/tomar) and past-tense norm. Classroom vocabulary, -mente adverbs, gender exceptions, learning procedures and prepositional pronouns are left out (they can be picked up as needed); everything else follows. Mastery checks favour role-play and real-document-scan tasks.

stages.title: Survival: greetings, food, shopping, getting around
Introducing yourself and talking about people
Daily life, likes and simple opinions
Travel problems: directions, favours, health, phone, services
Talking about your life: plans, experiences, stories
Comparing, discussing and the finer points

kcs.label: The Spanish alphabet and letter names
kcs.description: Spanish uses the Latin alphabet plus ñ (27 letters in the current academic list); ch and ll are digraphs, not separate letters. Each letter has a name (a, be, ce, de, e, efe, ge, hache, i, jota, ka, ele, eme, ene, eñe, o, pe, cu, erre, ese, te, u, uve, uve doble, equis, ye, zeta). Letter names are needed for spelling names, emails and codes.
forms: vowels: a e i o u
digraphs: ch, ll, rr, qu, gu
letters with more than one name: v = uve (also ve, ve baja/corta), w = uve doble (also doble ve; doble u in Mexico and parts of Central America), y = ye (also i griega)
letter names are feminine: la a, la be; plural: las aes, las bes

examples.es: ¿Cómo se escribe tu nombre? – Ene, a, de, i, a: Nadia.
examples.en: How do you spell your name? – N, A, D, I, A: Nadia.

examples.es: Mi apellido lleva eñe: Muñoz.
examples.en: My surname has an ñ: Muñoz.

mastery: Hearing a letter name, picks the right letter from a printed alphabet
Says the letters of their own name and surname without confusing e/i, g/j or r/rr
Writes down a 5–8 letter name or code spelled aloud at normal speed
commonErrors: EN: reads the letter name e as English "ee" and i as English "eye", so e and i are swapped
EN: names g and j with English values (g = "jee", j = "jay"); in Spanish g = ge /xe/ and j = jota
EN: treats h as pronounced; its name is hache and it is silent in words
boundaries: Letter names only; how letters sound inside words is kt:es-orth-sound-spelling
Spelling out loud as an interaction is kt:es-orth-spell-aloud

primitives.binding: Pairs of letter names English speakers confuse: e/i, g/j, a/e, r/erre; learner taps the letter heard, then says each so a partner can tell them apart
Hear a letter name and tap the letter card; younger learners point instead of writing

kcs.label: The five pure vowels
kcs.term: las vocales /a e i o u/
kcs.description: Spanish has five vowel sounds, each short, clear and never glided (o is not "oh-oo", e is not "ay-ee"). Unstressed vowels keep their quality instead of reducing to the English schwa. This is the single biggest change for English speakers and makes words recognisable.
forms: unstressed vowels keep full quality: chocolate = cho-co-la-te
diphthongs: ie, ue, ai, ei, au… in one syllable: bien, bueno, aire

examples.es: Tomo chocolate con leche.
examples.en: I have chocolate with milk.

examples.es: ¿Es su casa o mi casa?
examples.en: Is it his house or my house?

mastery: Hears the difference between minimal pairs that differ in one vowel (peso/piso/paso)
Reads aloud words of 3–4 syllables keeping every unstressed vowel full
Says their own name, city and a short sentence without gliding e and o
commonErrors: EN: reduces unstressed vowels to schwa: chocolate said as "chock-uh-lah-tee"
EN: glides e and o, so "no" sounds like English "know"
EN: pronounces final -e as silent or as "ee" (leche read as "leech")
boundaries: Consonants are kt:es-phon-consonants; stress placement is kt:es-phon-stress-syllables
Regional vowel features (e.g. weakened unstressed vowels in parts of Mexico) are not taught as targets

primitives.binding: Vowel minimal pairs peso/piso/paso, mesa/misa, todo/toda; learner picks what was heard, then records each so a listener can tell them apart
Learner records "chocolate", "teléfono", "leche", transcribes what a Spanish listener would hear, flags any vowel reduced to schwa

kcs.label: Spelling names and words aloud
kcs.description: Asking for and giving the spelling of names, streets and email addresses letter by letter. Useful phrases: ¿Cómo se escribe?, ¿Con be o con uve?, con hache, con tilde, arroba, punto.
forms: doble ele = ll, doble erre = rr

examples.es: ¿Cómo se escribe "Héctor"? – Con hache: hache, e con tilde, ce, te, o, erre.
examples.en: How do you spell "Héctor"? – With an h: h, e with an accent, c, t, o, r.

examples.es: Mi correo es ana punto ruiz arroba ejemplo punto com.
examples.en: My email is ana dot ruiz at example dot com.

mastery: Writes down a spelled surname or email correctly, including tildes and @
Spells their own full name and email so a listener writes it correctly
Asks ¿Cómo se escribe? or ¿Con be o con uve? when unsure in a form-filling role play
commonErrors: EN: says "at" and "dot" instead of arroba and punto
EN: forgets to mention the tilde, so the listener writes Hector
EN: spells ll as "el el" without saying doble ele or elle
boundaries: Letter names themselves are kt:es-orth-alphabet
Written accent rules are kt:es-orth-written-accents

primitives.binding: Hear spelled names and emails and type them into form fields; check h, b/v, ll, tildes and @ are right
Learner lacks a partner's surname and email and must get them with ¿Cómo se escribe? and check by reading back

kcs.label: Greeting, asking how someone is and saying goodbye
kcs.description: Fixed chunks to open and close an encounter. Spanish chooses the greeting by time of day: buenos días until lunch, buenas tardes until dark, buenas noches after dark (for both hello and goodbye). Hola works at any time and can be combined: Hola, buenos días.
forms: Hola. / Buenos días. / Buenas tardes. / Buenas noches.
Adiós. / Hasta luego. / Hasta mañana. / Hasta el lunes.
Chao / Chau (informal; common in much of Latin America)

examples.es: Buenos días, señora Gómez. – Buenos días.
examples.en: Good morning, Mrs Gómez. – Good morning.

examples.es: Hola, Luis, ¿qué tal? – Bien, ¿y tú? – Muy bien. ¡Hasta luego!
examples.en: Hi Luis, how are things? – Fine, and you? – Very well. See you later!

mastery: Chooses buenos días / buenas tardes / buenas noches for a given clock time
Answers ¿Qué tal? / ¿Cómo estás? and asks back
Opens and closes a short meeting in a role play with greeting, how-are-you and a goodbye that names the next meeting
commonErrors: EN: says *Buenos tardes (gender: buenas tardes, buenos días)
EN: uses buenas noches only as "good night" and avoids it as an evening hello
EN: answers ¿Qué tal? with a long account; a short Bien, ¿y tú? is expected
boundaries: tú vs usted choices are kt:es-soc-tu-usted; kisses and handshakes are kt:es-soc-greeting-customs
Greeting formulas in letters (Querido/a…) are kt:es-act-letters-emails

primitives.binding: Greeting–how-are-you–goodbye turns; branches by clock time (9:00 / 16:00 / 22:00) check that the greeting matches the time and that the learner asks back
Hola, ¿qué tal? to a classmate vs Buenos días, ¿cómo está? to an older neighbour; learner marks which one sounds too casual

kcs.label: Thanking, apologising and small social formulas
kcs.description: High-frequency formulas: thanking and replying, apologising (perdón for small slips, lo siento for regret), and a few ritual phrases such as ¡Salud! when toasting.

examples.es: Muchas gracias. – De nada.
examples.en: Thank you very much. – You're welcome.

examples.es: Perdón, ¿es su bolso? – Sí, gracias.
examples.en: Sorry, is this your bag? – Yes, thanks.

mastery: Matches gracias / perdón / lo siento / ¡salud! to pictured situations
Replies to thanks and to an apology with an appropriate formula
Uses at least two formulas naturally in a café or street role play
commonErrors: EN: uses lo siento to get past someone (perdón or con permiso is used)
EN: says *De nada as a reply to an apology (use No pasa nada / Vale)
EN: transfers "I'm sorry" for sympathy and for bumping into someone with one form only
boundaries: Attention-getters perdona/perdone, oye/oiga are kt:es-fn-attention-getters
Congratulations and good wishes are kt:es-fn-celebrations-wishes

primitives.binding: Short incidents (bump into someone, receive help, toast at dinner); learner picks the formula and the reply; branch shows reaction to lo siento vs perdón
Learner thanks a waiter for every plate in a long string of gracias, or never thanks a friend: judge how each lands

kcs.label: Asking someone to repeat, slow down or explain
kcs.description: When understanding breaks down, a few fixed phrases keep the conversation going: asking for repetition, slower speech, the meaning of a word or how to say something.

examples.es: Perdón, no entiendo. ¿Puede repetir, por favor?
examples.en: Sorry, I don't understand. Can you repeat, please?

examples.es: ¿Cómo se dice "receipt" en español? – Tique o recibo.
examples.en: How do you say "receipt" in Spanish? – Tique or recibo.

mastery: Recognises when the other person is asking for repetition
Produces three different repair phrases from memory
In a simulated conversation uses a repair phrase instead of falling silent when lost
commonErrors: EN: says *¿Qué? abruptly; ¿Cómo? or ¿Perdón? is softer
EN: says *Repite instead of ¿Puedes repetir?, which sounds like an order
EN: *No comprendo used for everything; fine, but No entiendo is more common in speech
boundaries: Gestures and compensating with simple words are kt:es-str-nonverbal
Can (poder) as a grammar point is kt:es-poder-permission-ability; here ¿Puedes…? is a fixed chunk

primitives.binding: Audio that speeds up or drops a key word; learner must use ¿Puede repetir?/Más despacio before answering; check repair is asked, not guessed
Directions or price exchange where the partner speaks too fast; branch only continues after a repair phrase

kcs.label: Gestures, nonverbal signals and compensating
kcs.description: At A1 meaning is often carried by gesture plus a word: pointing with esto, por favor; shaking the head; así así with a rocking hand; shh for silence; looking at the watch to close. Learners need to read these signals and use simple words to compensate.
forms: por favor + pointing at the thing
closing signals: looking at the watch, gathering things
compensating: una cosa para… (a thing for…)

examples.es: Esto, por favor. (señalando)
examples.en: This one, please. (pointing)

examples.es: ¿Qué tal el examen? – Así, así. (moviendo la mano)
examples.en: How was the exam? – So-so. (rocking the hand)

mastery: Interprets common gestures in short video clips
Combines a gesture with a word to ask for an object they cannot name
In a role play, closes a conversation or asks for silence using a gesture plus a formula
commonErrors: EN: uses English "OK" circle gestures or thumbs-up assuming identical meaning everywhere
EN: waits silently when a word is missing instead of compensating with una cosa para…
boundaries: Spoken repair phrases are kt:es-str-repair-basic
Regional differences in gesture meaning are only flagged, not taught

primitives.binding: Short clips of gestures (así así, shh, watch-glance); learner says what the speaker meant and what reply fits
Learner must get an object they cannot name by pointing plus esto/eso, por favor, or una cosa para…; check the right object is obtained

levels.locator: PCIC · Funciones · Inventario A1-A2 · 2.5 · columna A1

kcs.label: How letters sound: regular sound–spelling rules
kcs.description: Spanish spelling is close to phonetic, so once a few rules are known every word can be read aloud. Key rules: c = /k/ before a, o, u and /θ/ (Spain) or /s/ (Latin America, Canarias, parts of Andalusia) before e, i; qu = /k/ before e, i; g = /g/ before a, o, u and /x/ before e, i; gu = /g/ before e, i; j = /x/; h is silent; ll and y sound the same for most speakers; ñ = /ɲ/; b and v sound the same; rr and initial r are trilled.
forms: ca co cu / que qui / ce ci (za zo zu)
ga go gu / gue gui / ge gi = je ji
b and v are both /b/: vaso, beso
r between vowels: pero; rr and initial r: perro, Roma

examples.es: Cecilia come queso en el cine.
examples.en: Cecilia eats cheese at the cinema.

examples.es: Gema y Hugo juegan con el gato.
examples.en: Gema and Hugo are playing with the cat.

mastery: Reads aloud unseen regular words (guerra, cine, hijo, llave) with the right sounds
Writes simple dictated words with c/qu, g/gu/j, h and ñ correctly
Predicts the pronunciation of a new place name from its spelling
commonErrors: EN: pronounces h (hola as "hola" with English h)
EN: reads j and ge/gi as English j ("Juan" as "jwan")
EN: reads ll as English l (llamo as "lamo")
EN: reads que/qui with a w sound ("kway")
boundaries: Sounds that need articulation practice (trill, /x/, /θ/) are kt:es-phon-consonants
Spelling choices for the same sound (b/v, g/j, ll/y) are only partly predictable; A2 rules are in kt:es-orth-spelling-a2

primitives.binding: Map ca/que/qui/co/cu and ga/gue/gui/ge/gi letter by letter to sounds, blend new words (guitarra, cigüeña excluded), then spell heard words
Learner states the c/qu and g/gu rule, then applies it to unseen place names (Quito, Guernica, Cuenca); system shows which rule each step used

kcs.label: Subject pronouns and dropping them
kcs.term: yo, tú, él, ella, usted, nosotros…
kcs.description: Spanish subject pronouns are yo, tú, él, ella, usted, nosotros/as, vosotros/as, ellos/as, ustedes. Because the verb ending already shows the person, the pronoun is usually left out; it is used for contrast or emphasis (Yo soy Ana, ¿y tú?). There is no subject pronoun for things or for "it": the verb alone is used.
forms: Spain: vosotros = informal plural you; Latin America and Canarias: ustedes for all plural you
voseo: vos instead of tú in Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, Central America and elsewhere (recognition only)
pro-drop: Soy de Lima. (not *Yo soy… every time)

examples.es: Yo soy de Chile, ¿y tú? – Yo, de Perú.
examples.en: I'm from Chile, and you? – Me, from Peru.

examples.es: Mi hermana se llama Lucía y vive en Sevilla.
examples.en: My sister is called Lucía and (she) lives in Seville.

mastery: Identifies the person from verb endings when no pronoun is present
Leaves out the pronoun in neutral sentences and uses it for contrast
Chooses ellos vs ellas and nosotros vs nosotras for mixed and all-female groups
commonErrors: EN: repeats yo in every sentence, which sounds insistent
EN: invents *ello or uses él for things ("*Él es grande" for a table)
EN: uses ellos for an all-female group (ellas is needed)
boundaries: Object pronouns are kt:es-direct-object-pronouns and kt:es-indirect-object-pronouns
Choosing tú/usted is kt:es-soc-tu-usted; voseo verb forms are recognised but not produced

primitives.binding: Sentences without subject pronouns (Vivimos en Quito / Viven en Quito); learner must say who, using only the verb ending
Three-sentence text about a family; learner links each dropped subject to the right person

kcs.label: Ser in the present: identity, origin and profession
kcs.description: Ser (soy, eres, es, somos, sois, son) links a subject to who or what it is: name, nationality, origin (ser de), profession and type. Professions after ser normally take no article: Soy profesora.
forms: soy, eres, es, somos, sois, son
ser + nationality/profession: Es mexicano. Soy estudiante.
ser de + place: Somos de Bogotá.
no article with profession: Es médico. (not *Es un médico, unless qualified)

examples.es: Soy Tomás y soy de Valencia.
examples.en: I'm Tomás and I'm from Valencia.

examples.es: ¿Sois estudiantes? – No, somos profesores.
examples.en: Are you (all) students? – No, we're teachers.

mastery: Selects the correct form of ser for each person
Introduces themselves and a classmate with name, origin and occupation
Corrects wrong information about someone using No, no es…, es…
commonErrors: EN: adds an article before professions: *Soy una estudiante
EN: uses estar for origin or identity: *Estoy de Londres
ZH: omits the verb altogether in "I student" type sentences
boundaries: Estar for location is kt:es-estar-location; the ser/estar contrast for adjectives is kt:es-ser-vs-estar
Describing appearance with ser + adjective is kt:es-describe-people

primitives.binding: Learner fills the ser grid, then applies it to new subjects (mi madre y yo, Pedro y tú); each step shows which person the form encodes
Learner has ID cards with missing nationality or job and must ask ¿Eres…? / ¿De dónde es…? to complete them

kcs.label: Countries, nationalities and languages
kcs.description: Names of countries and the adjectives for nationality and language. Nationality adjectives agree in gender and number and are written with a lower-case letter: español/española, mexicano/mexicana, estadounidense. Language names usually equal the masculine adjective: hablo inglés.
forms: consonant + -a: español/española, inglés/inglesa, alemán/alemana (accent drops in feminine)
languages: el español (also castellano), el inglés, el chino
lower case: español, francés; capital only for countries: España
countries without article: España, México; El Salvador keeps it

examples.es: Ella es colombiana, pero vive en Londres.
examples.en: She is Colombian, but she lives in London.

examples.es: Hablo inglés y un poco de español.
examples.en: I speak English and a little Spanish.

mastery: Matches countries, nationality adjectives and languages
Writes masculine and feminine forms of 10 nationalities with correct accents and lower case
Says their own and a partner's nationality and languages
commonErrors: EN: capitalises nationalities and languages: *Inglés, *Español
EN: keeps the accent in the feminine: *inglésa, *francésa
EN: says *americano for US-only identity; estadounidense is the precise term (americano is often understood as of the Americas)
boundaries: Agreement as a general rule is kt:es-adjective-agreement
Spanish vs castellano as language names and regional varieties are in kt:es-soc-variety-awareness

primitives.binding: Country shown, learner types masculine and feminine nationality before the answer appears; first attempt kept
Rule -o/-a vs consonant + a vs invariable; apply to unseen nationalities (portugués, japonés, belga)

kcs.label: Introducing yourself and others
kcs.description: Saying your name (Me llamo…, Soy…), introducing others (Este es…, Esta es…; at A2 Te presento a… / Le presento a…) and replying (Encantado/a, Mucho gusto, Hola, ¿qué tal?). Also confirming identity: ¿Eres Ana? – Sí, soy yo.
forms: Este es Juan. / Esta es Marta.
Te presento a… / Le presento a… (A2)
¿El señor Ruiz, por favor? – Sí, soy yo.

examples.es: Hola, me llamo Pablo. – Encantada, yo soy Inés.
examples.en: Hi, my name is Pablo. – Nice to meet you, I'm Inés.

examples.es: Mamá, esta es Carmen, mi compañera de clase.
examples.en: Mum, this is Carmen, my classmate.

mastery: Chooses este/esta according to the person introduced
Uses encantado vs encantada according to their own gender
Performs a three-person introduction role play, formal and informal
commonErrors: EN: says *Mi nombre es… all the time; correct but Me llamo… is more natural in speech
EN: a woman says *encantado (agreement with the speaker: encantada)
EN: *Te presento Luis without a (personal a is needed with people)
boundaries: Asking for other personal data is kt:es-fn-personal-details
Register choice is kt:es-soc-tu-usted; reflexive llamarse is used as a chunk here, its grammar is kt:es-reflexive-verbs

primitives.binding: Party scene: learner introduces themself, then a friend to a third person; branch checks este/esta and encantado/a against the characters
Same introduction to a classmate (Este es…) and to a new boss (Le presento a la señora…); learner flags the mismatched version

kcs.label: Tú or usted: addressing people
kcs.description: Spanish marks social distance in the verb: tú (informal) vs usted (formal, takes 3rd-person verb forms). Plural: vosotros (informal, Spain only) vs ustedes (formal in Spain; all plural "you" in Latin America and Canarias). Titles: señor/señora + surname (Sr. López), don/doña + first name for respect. Use of tú is wide in Spain; usted is more frequent in many Latin American countries.
forms: señor, señora, señorita (less used now) + surname
abbreviations: Sr., Sra., D., D.ª, Ud./Vd., Uds.

examples.es: Perdone, señora, ¿usted es la profesora? – Sí, soy yo.
examples.en: Excuse me, madam, are you the teacher? – Yes, I am.

examples.es: ¿Vosotros sois de Madrid? / ¿Ustedes son de Madrid?
examples.en: Are you (pl.) from Madrid? (Spain informal / Latin America or formal)

mastery: Identifies whether a sentence addresses someone as tú or usted from the verb form
Rewrites a short request from tú to usted, changing verb and possessive forms
Chooses tú or usted for six pictured situations and justifies the choice
commonErrors: EN: uses usted with 2nd-person verb: *¿Usted eres…?
EN: uses vosotros forms with Latin American interlocutors, or never recognises vosotros in Spanish media
EN: says señor + first name (*Señor Juan) where don Juan or señor Pérez is expected
boundaries: Politeness by indirectness (¿Me pones…?, conditional) is kt:es-fn-requests-favours
Voseo is recognised in kt:es-soc-variety-awareness, not produced

primitives.binding: Same question to a child, a classmate, a hotel receptionist and an elderly neighbour; learner sets tú/usted and checks verb form agrees
Sentences where only the verb ending shows tú vs usted (¿Habla inglés? / ¿Hablas inglés?); learner decides who is being addressed

kcs.label: Greeting customs: kisses, handshakes and personal space
kcs.description: In Spain friends and new acquaintances (especially women, or men greeting women) often exchange two kisses on the cheek; in much of Latin America one kiss is common. Handshakes are used in formal and business contexts and between men. People tend to stand closer and touch arms more than in many English-speaking cultures.
forms: dar dos besos (Spain) / un beso (much of Latin America)
un abrazo (hug, friends; also written sign-off)
greeting everyone when entering a small shop or lift: Buenos días

examples.es: En España, al conocer a alguien, muchas veces se dan dos besos.
examples.en: In Spain, when meeting someone, people often give two kisses.

examples.es: En la entrevista de trabajo le doy la mano.
examples.en: In the job interview I shake hands with him/her.

mastery: Describes which greeting gesture fits family, friends, a business meeting, in Spain and in one Latin American country
Judges a short scenario in which a visitor's greeting causes awkwardness
Explains one difference from their own culture
commonErrors: EN: pulls back from the cheek kiss, read as coldness
EN: assumes one custom for all Spanish-speaking countries
boundaries: Verbal greeting formulas are kt:es-fn-greetings
Customs vary by country, region, age and setting; statements here are tendencies, not rules

primitives.binding: Visitor offers a handshake to a friend's mother at a family meal in Seville; learner explains the reading and rewrites the moment
Grid of situations × countries (Spain, Mexico, Argentina): learner predicts kisses/handshake, then compares with the provided notes

kcs.label: Spanish around the world: main variety differences
kcs.description: Spanish is spoken as an official language in about 20 countries. Educated speakers understand each other easily, but learners should recognise the main differences: vosotros (Spain) vs ustedes (Latin America); distinción of /θ/ vs seseo; yeísmo; voseo (vos tienes → vos tenés) in the River Plate and Central America; some vocabulary (coche/carro/auto, ordenador/computadora, móvil/celular, zumo/jugo). No variety is more "correct".
forms: lexical pairs: coche/carro, ordenador/computadora, móvil/celular, zumo/jugo, piso/apartamento/departamento
español and castellano both name the language

examples.es: En México dicen "carro" o "coche"; en Argentina, "auto".
examples.en: In Mexico they say "carro" or "coche"; in Argentina, "auto".

examples.es: ¿Vos sos de Buenos Aires? = ¿Tú eres de Buenos Aires?
examples.en: Are you from Buenos Aires? (voseo = tú form)

mastery: Identifies vosotros, voseo and seseo in short recordings or texts
Matches common lexical pairs between Spain and Latin America
Chooses one variety as their production model and stays consistent within a text
commonErrors: EN: mixes forms inconsistently (vosotros with Latin American vocabulary) in one text
EN: believes one variety is the "real" Spanish and dismisses others
boundaries: The course models a general standard; regional forms are taught for recognition unless a track chooses a variety
Detailed dialect phonetics and the full voseo paradigm are beyond A2

primitives.binding: Same short dialogue in Madrid, Mexico City and Buenos Aires versions; learner marks vosotros/ustedes, seseo/distinción, coche/carro/auto, vos
Hear a speaker and tap the region on a map; first-attempt choice kept, then explanation of the clue

kcs.label: The Spanish-speaking world: countries, capitals, currencies and symbols
kcs.description: Basic cultural reference knowledge: where Spanish is spoken, capitals, a few currencies (euro, peso, sol, bolívar…), forms of government (monarchy in Spain, republics elsewhere), official and co-official languages (Catalan, Galician, Basque in Spain; Quechua, Guaraní, Aymara and others in Latin America), large cities and famous places.
forms: países y capitales: Madrid, Ciudad de México, Bogotá, Lima, Buenos Aires…
monedas: el euro, el peso, el sol, el colón…
lenguas cooficiales: catalán, gallego, euskera; quechua, guaraní…

examples.es: La capital de Perú es Lima y la moneda es el sol.
examples.en: The capital of Peru is Lima and the currency is the sol.

examples.es: En Paraguay se hablan español y guaraní.
examples.en: In Paraguay people speak Spanish and Guaraní.

mastery: Places 10 Spanish-speaking countries on a map and names their capitals
Reads a short fact card about a country and answers questions
Gives a 4–5 sentence spoken profile of one country
commonErrors: EN: thinks Spanish is only spoken in Spain and Mexico
EN: assumes Brazil is Spanish-speaking
boundaries: Facts change (currencies, government); a teacher should keep figures current
History and the arts are kt:es-cult-society-arts

primitives.binding: A country fact sheet; learner finds capital, currency, languages and population needed for a quiz card
Two partners each hold half the facts about three countries and must ask ¿Cuál es la capital de…? ¿Qué lenguas se hablan en…?

kcs.label: Intonation of statements and questions
kcs.description: Statements fall at the end. Yes/no questions usually rise at the end, and because word order often stays the same, intonation alone can turn a statement into a question (Eres de aquí. / ¿Eres de aquí?). Questions with a question word (¿Dónde vives?) normally fall. Spanish intonation is flatter in the middle of the phrase than English.

examples.es: Hablas español. / ¿Hablas español?
examples.en: You speak Spanish. / Do you speak Spanish?

examples.es: ¿Cómo te llamas? – Me llamo Rosa.
examples.en: What's your name? – My name is Rosa.

mastery: Hears whether a sentence is a statement or a yes/no question
Produces the same words as a statement and as a question with the right melody
Asks and answers personal questions with natural intonation in a short dialogue
commonErrors: EN: adds English-style do-support words or changes word order instead of using intonation
EN: rises at the end of wh-questions, sounding surprised or impatient
boundaries: Question marks in writing are kt:es-orth-inverted-marks
Fine regional intonation patterns (e.g. Mexican or Argentine) are not modelled

primitives.binding: Hear "Hablas español" with rise or fall; learner picks the contour and the punctuation, then says it with the matching melody
Minimal pairs of melody only (Es tarde. / ¿Es tarde?); learner must produce the version a partner identifies

kcs.label: Opening question and exclamation marks
kcs.description: Spanish opens questions and exclamations with inverted marks (¿, ¡) placed exactly where the question or exclamation starts, which may be mid-sentence. No full stop follows the closing mark. Question words carry a written accent (qué, dónde, cómo).
forms: no full stop after ? or !: ¿Vienes? Sí.
question words with accent: qué, quién, cómo, dónde, cuándo, cuánto

examples.es: Perdona, ¿dónde está el baño?
examples.en: Excuse me, where is the bathroom?

examples.es: ¡Qué bien! ¿Vienes mañana?
examples.en: Great! Are you coming tomorrow?

mastery: Spots missing ¿ or ¡ in short texts
Places the opening mark at the right point in sentences that start with a vocative or a connector
Writes a five-question interview with correct punctuation and accents on question words
commonErrors: EN: omits the opening marks entirely
EN: puts ¿ at the start of the whole sentence even when the question starts later
EN: writes que, donde, como without accent in questions
boundaries: Accent rules in general are kt:es-orth-written-accents
Other punctuation is kt:es-orth-capitals-punctuation

primitives.binding: Learner's own chat message: fix only ¿/¡ placement first, then only accents on question words
Sentences where the position of ¿ changes what is asked (Y tú, ¿vienes? / ¿Y tú vienes?); learner places it

kcs.label: Numbers 0–100
kcs.description: Cardinal numbers from cero to cien. 16–29 are written as one word (dieciséis, veintidós); from 31 the tens and units are joined by y (treinta y uno). Uno becomes un before a masculine noun and una before a feminine one.
forms: 30–99: treinta y uno, cuarenta y cinco…
un libro / una casa / veintiún años
phone numbers read in pairs or singly: 91 578 84 67

examples.es: Tengo veintitrés años.
examples.en: I am twenty-three years old.

examples.es: Mi teléfono es el seis, cero, cinco, cuarenta y dos, treinta y uno, diecisiete.
examples.en: My phone number is 6, 0, 5, 42, 31, 17.

mastery: Writes numbers heard at natural speed, including the 12/2, 13/30 and 15/50 type confusions (doce/dos, trece/treinta)
Reads aloud prices, ages and phone numbers
Exchanges phone numbers and checks them by reading back
commonErrors: EN: *veinte y dos instead of veintidós
EN: confuses seis/siete and trece/treinta when listening
EN: *uno libro instead of un libro
boundaries: Hundreds, thousands and millions are kt:es-numbers-large; ordinals are kt:es-ordinals
Writing conventions for decimals and thousands are in kt:es-numbers-large

primitives.binding: Phone numbers, ages and room numbers read aloud; learner fills slots; errors grouped as teen/ten, 6/7, pairs vs single digits
Digits flash; learner says the number before audio confirms; first attempt kept

kcs.label: Tener in the present: having and age
kcs.description: Tener (tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tenéis, tienen) expresses possession, family, features and age: Tengo dos hermanos. Tiene treinta años. Spanish uses tener, not ser/estar, for age. The irregular forms are learned as whole words at this stage.
forms: tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tenéis, tienen
negative without article: No tengo hermanos.
short answer: ¿Tienes coche? – No, no tengo.

examples.es: ¿Cuántos años tiene tu abuela? – Tiene ochenta y dos.
examples.en: How old is your grandmother? – She's eighty-two.

examples.es: Mi piso tiene dos habitaciones.
examples.en: My flat has two bedrooms.

mastery: Chooses tener rather than ser for age in a mixed set
Produces all forms of tener in a fill-in grid
Asks and answers about age, siblings and pets in a class survey
commonErrors: EN: *Soy veinte años (calque of "I am 20")
EN: keeps the article in negatives and questions: *No tengo un hermano (No tengo hermanos is the natural form)
EN: over-applies the stem change: *tienemos for tenemos, or regularises: *teno for tengo
boundaries: Tener que for obligation is kt:es-tener-que-hay-que; tener hambre/frío is kt:es-tener-sensations-doler
The general stem-change pattern (e>ie) is kt:es-present-stem-change

primitives.binding: Mixed sentences about age, nationality and location; learner must pick tener / ser / estar by meaning, not by English verb
Class survey: learner must ask ¿Cuántos años tienes? ¿Tienes hermanos? and fill a table

kcs.label: Question words: qué, quién, dónde, cómo, cuánto, por qué
kcs.description: Question words go at the start, carry a written accent and are often followed directly by the verb (¿Dónde vives?). Cuánto agrees with the noun (cuántos años, cuántas hermanas). Quién asks about people, qué about things and actions.
forms: verb follows the question word: ¿Dónde vive Marta?

examples.es: ¿De dónde es tu profesor? – Es de Uruguay.
examples.en: Where is your teacher from? – He's from Uruguay.

examples.es: ¿Cuántas lenguas hablas?
examples.en: How many languages do you speak?

mastery: Matches question words with possible answers
Writes the question that produces a given answer
Interviews a classmate with at least six different question words
commonErrors: EN: keeps English order: *¿Dónde Marta vive?
EN: uses *cuánto años without agreement
EN: *¿Cómo es tu nombre? (calque) instead of ¿Cómo te llamas?
boundaries: Cuál vs qué, cuándo, para qué and prepositions + question words are kt:es-interrogatives-a2
Porque vs por qué is kt:es-porque-por-que

primitives.binding: Drag question word, verb and subject into slots; violating order (¿Dónde Marta vive?) names the rule: verb right after the question word
Learner must find out four facts about a character by asking; only well-formed questions get answers

kcs.label: Asking for and giving personal details
kcs.description: Asking and answering about name, age, address, phone, email, job and studies, as at a reception desk or when registering. Answers can be short (Quince. / En la calle Mayor.).
forms: ¿Cuál es tu número de teléfono? / tu correo?
¿A qué te dedicas? / ¿Qué haces? – Soy…/ Estudio…
address order: calle + name + number + floor: c/ Mayor, 5, 2.º

examples.es: ¿Dónde vives? – En la avenida de América, número doce.
examples.en: Where do you live? – On Avenida de América, number twelve.

examples.es: ¿A qué te dedicas? – Soy enfermera.
examples.en: What do you do? – I'm a nurse.

mastery: Picks the right answer to each personal-data question
Completes a registration form from a recorded dialogue
Plays both receptionist and guest in a check-in role play
commonErrors: EN: *¿Qué es tu número? (cuál is needed before es + noun)
EN: gives address in English order (number first)
EN: *Trabajo como un profesor (Soy profesor / Trabajo de profesor)
boundaries: Names and surnames customs are kt:es-soc-names-surnames
Filling written forms as a genre is kt:es-act-reading-signs-forms

primitives.binding: Hotel check-in: learner (receptionist) must obtain name, ID number, phone and email; asked questions are logged
A real-looking registration form (nombre, apellidos, domicilio, C.P., teléfono); each field constrains what is written

kcs.label: Names and two surnames
kcs.description: People in Spanish-speaking countries usually have one or two given names and two surnames: the father's first surname and the mother's first surname (Spain now allows either order). Women do not change surnames on marriage. Compound first names are common (José Luis, María José), and short forms are used among friends (Pepe for José, Paco for Francisco, Lola for Dolores).
forms: nombre + primer apellido + segundo apellido: Ana García Pérez
forms ask for nombre and apellidos
hipocorísticos: Pepe, Paco, Lola, Charo; Latin America also Pancho, Chayo
particles in lower case: Miguel de Cervantes, Enrique de la Rosa

examples.es: Me llamo Lucía Martín Ortega: Martín es de mi padre y Ortega, de mi madre.
examples.en: My name is Lucía Martín Ortega: Martín is my father's and Ortega my mother's.

examples.es: Se llama Francisco, pero todos le dicen Paco.
examples.en: His name is Francisco, but everyone calls him Paco.

mastery: Identifies first name, father's surname and mother's surname in a full name
Fills in "nombre" and "apellidos" on a form correctly for a Spanish name
Explains how a child's surnames are formed from the parents' names
commonErrors: EN: treats the second surname as a middle name and drops the first surname
EN: addresses someone by their mother's surname alone
boundaries: Address titles (señor, don) are kt:es-soc-tu-usted
Legal rules on surname order differ by country; only the general pattern is taught

primitives.binding: A booking under "Carmen Ruiz López" cannot be found under "López"; learner explains why and how to ask for it
Scan ID-card mock-ups and forms; find nombre, primer apellido and segundo apellido

kcs.label: Key consonants: r and rr, j, ñ, b/v, d, z/c
kcs.description: Spanish consonants that differ from English: the tap r (pero) vs the trill rr (perro); /x/ for j and ge/gi (a strong h from the back of the mouth, softer in the Caribbean and Andalusia); ñ; b and v both /b/, softened between vowels; d softened between vowels (cada); p, t, k without the English puff of air; z and ce/ci = /θ/ in most of Spain, /s/ elsewhere.
forms: r at word start = trill: Roma, rojo
b = v: vino, bien; soft between vowels: lobo, uva
d soft between vowels: nada, cada

examples.es: El perro de Rosa corre por la carretera.
examples.en: Rosa's dog runs along the road.

examples.es: Mi hijo come jamón en junio.
examples.en: My son eats ham in June.

mastery: Distinguishes pero/perro and caro/carro by ear
Produces a tap and a trill so a listener can tell pero from perro
Reads a short tongue twister with r/rr and j at a steady pace
commonErrors: EN: uses English r for both r and rr
EN: aspirates p, t, k (puff of air) so Spanish listeners hear a foreign accent
EN: pronounces v as English /v/
EN: hard English d between vowels (nada)
boundaries: Spelling of these sounds is kt:es-orth-sound-spelling
Seseo and distinción are both correct models; a learner chooses one (see kt:es-soc-variety-awareness)

primitives.binding: Minimal pairs pero/perro, caro/carro, ano/año; learner picks what was heard, then must produce each so a listener scores it
Learner records "El perro de Rosa…", transcribes what a listener hears and marks any English r or /v/

kcs.label: Noun gender
kcs.description: Every Spanish noun is masculine or feminine. Most nouns in -o are masculine and in -a feminine; nouns in -e or a consonant must be learned with their article. For people, gender often follows the person (el amigo / la amiga, el padre / la madre). Shortened words keep the original gender: la foto, la moto, la radio.
forms: learn with article: el árbol, la catedral, el coche, la noche
people: el amigo / la amiga, el profesor / la profesora
irregular pairs: el padre / la madre, el hombre / la mujer

examples.es: La foto de la clase está en la mesa.
examples.en: The class photo is on the table.

examples.es: Mi profesora es de Cuba y mi profesor es de Chile.
examples.en: My (female) teacher is from Cuba and my (male) teacher is from Chile.

mastery: Sorts 30 common nouns into masculine and feminine
Gives the feminine of people nouns (amigo, profesor, vecino)
Uses the right article with new nouns met in a text, guessing from the ending and checking
commonErrors: EN: assumes all -e nouns are one gender
EN: *el foto, *el mano (both feminine: la foto, la mano)
ZH and EN: forgets that gender is grammatical, not only for people
boundaries: Exceptions such as el día, el problema, la mano and el agua are kt:es-noun-gender-exceptions
Agreement with adjectives is kt:es-adjective-agreement

primitives.binding: Learner states the -o/-a and -ción tendencies, then applies them to unseen nouns; the system shows which rule each choice used and flags guesses on -e/consonant
Judge el/la with problema, mano, día, foto, mapa: which follow the tendency and which are exceptions

kcs.label: Plural of nouns
kcs.description: Nouns ending in a vowel add -s (casa → casas); nouns ending in a consonant add -es (árbol → árboles, país → países). Nouns ending in -z change to -ces (luz → luces). Nouns in unstressed -s do not change (el lunes / los lunes). Some nouns are normally plural: las gafas, los pantalones.
forms: consonant + es: ciudad → ciudades, profesor → profesores
unstressed -s: el lunes → los lunes, la crisis → las crisis
accent may change: canción → canciones, joven → jóvenes

examples.es: Tengo dos lápices y tres cuadernos.
examples.en: I have two pencils and three notebooks.

examples.es: Los lunes y los martes tengo clase.
examples.en: On Mondays and Tuesdays I have class.

mastery: Forms the plural of 20 nouns including -z and accented endings
Spots plural errors in a shopping list
Describes what is in their bag or room using plurals
commonErrors: EN: *lápizes (z changes to c)
EN: *ciudads (needs -es)
EN: keeps the accent: *canciónes
boundaries: Article and adjective agreement in the plural are kt:es-articles and kt:es-adjective-agreement
Accent changes follow kt:es-orth-written-accents

primitives.binding: Rule: vowel +s / consonant +es / z→ces; apply to unseen nouns (pez, avión, autobús, sofá) with each step shown
Picture of a desk: learner lists objects with numbers; check plural endings and that numbers match the picture

kcs.label: Definite and indefinite articles
kcs.term: el, la, los, las / un, una, unos, unas
kcs.description: Articles agree with the noun in gender and number. a + el → al and de + el → del. The indefinite article introduces something new (Tengo un perro), the definite one refers to something known or unique (El perro es negro). Spanish uses the definite article with nouns in general statements and with gustar (Me gusta el café) but not with first names (María, not *la María in standard speech).
forms: el libro, la mesa, los libros, las mesas
un libro, una mesa, unos libros, unas mesas
al = a + el; del = de + el
new vs known: Hay un gato. El gato es gris.
no article with names: Ana es mi amiga.
no article with ser + profession: Es médico.

examples.es: Tengo un perro y una gata. El perro se llama Max.
examples.en: I have a dog and a cat. The dog is called Max.

examples.es: Voy al cine con la hermana de Pedro.
examples.en: I'm going to the cinema with Pedro's sister.

mastery: Chooses el/la/los/las and un/una/unos/unas for nouns of known gender
Uses al and del whenever required
In a short text, uses indefinite for first mention and definite for second mention
commonErrors: EN: *a el cine, *de el libro (contraction is obligatory)
EN: omits the article in general statements: *Me gusta café
EN: *Soy un profesor (no article with bare profession)
boundaries: Hay + indefinite vs estar + definite is kt:es-hay-vs-estar
el agua, generic uses and approximation unos 50 euros are kt:es-article-uses-a2

primitives.binding: Same picture story: learner chooses un/el for each mention and sees how the meaning (new vs already known) changes
Sentences where only the article tells whether the listener knows the object (¿Tienes un bolígrafo? / ¿Tienes el bolígrafo?)

kcs.label: Adjectives: agreement and position
kcs.description: Adjectives agree with the noun in gender and number and usually follow it: un coche rojo, unas casas grandes. Adjectives in -o change to -a; those in -e or most consonants have one form for both genders (interesante, fácil); nationality adjectives in a consonant add -a. Plural adds -s or -es.
forms: position: noun + adjective: una película divertida
ser + adjective agrees with the subject: Mis amigas son simpáticas.
not with possessive + adjective alone: *mi guapo

examples.es: Vivo en una casa pequeña con un jardín bonito.
examples.en: I live in a small house with a nice garden.

examples.es: Las clases son interesantes pero difíciles.
examples.en: The classes are interesting but difficult.

mastery: Makes adjectives agree in a fill-in exercise with mixed genders and numbers
Corrects agreement errors in a short description
Writes a five-sentence description of their room or town with correct agreement
commonErrors: EN: puts the adjective before the noun: *un rojo coche
EN: forgets plural agreement: *las casas grande
EN: *interesanta (adjectives in -e have no feminine -a)
boundaries: Comparatives are kt:es-comparatives; muy/mucho is kt:es-muy-mucho
Meaning changes with pre-nominal position (un gran hombre) are B1

primitives.binding: Agreement rule for -o, -e and consonant adjectives; apply to unseen adjective–noun pairs (una calle ancha, unos coches azules)
Describe a picture of a street; check each adjective agrees with the noun it is attached to and matches the picture

kcs.label: Demonstratives: este, ese, aquel and esto, eso
kcs.description: Spanish has three distances: este (near me), ese (near you / not far), aquel (far from both). They agree with the noun and come before it. The neuter forms esto, eso, aquello refer to something unidentified (¿Qué es esto?). Demonstratives can stand alone: Quiero ese.

examples.es: ¿Qué es esto? – Es un abanico.
examples.en: What is this? – It's a fan.

examples.es: No quiero esta camiseta; quiero aquella, la azul.
examples.en: I don't want this T-shirt; I want that one over there, the blue one.

mastery: Chooses este/ese/aquel for objects at three distances in a picture
Uses esto/eso for unknown objects and the agreeing form for known ones
Picks objects in a shop role play by pointing and naming
commonErrors: EN: two-way thinking (this/that), never uses aquel
EN: *esto libro (neuter cannot go with a noun)
EN: *el este libro (article and demonstrative together)
boundaries: Spatial adverbs aquí/ahí/allí are kt:es-place-expressions
Anaphoric use (este = the latter) is beyond A2 production

primitives.binding: Scene with speaker, listener and objects at three distances; learner moves the speaker and must re-choose este/ese/aquel
Hear "Dame ese libro" etc. and tap the object at the right distance from the speaker

kcs.label: Classroom language and objects
kcs.description: Words and chunks to run a lesson in Spanish: objects (libro, cuaderno, bolígrafo, lápiz, goma, pizarra, ordenador), instructions (lee, escucha, escribe, completa, en parejas) and learner phrases (¿Cómo se dice…?, ¿Cómo se escribe…?, ¿En qué página?, No entiendo).
forms: el libro, el cuaderno, el bolígrafo/boli, el lápiz, la goma, el diccionario, la pizarra
abrid el libro, escuchad, leed, escribid (vosotros) / abran, escuchen (ustedes)

examples.es: ¿Cómo se dice "rubber" en español? – Goma.
examples.en: How do you say "rubber" in Spanish? – Goma.

examples.es: Trabajad en parejas y completad la tabla.
examples.en: Work in pairs and complete the table.

mastery: Follows ten common classroom instructions without translation
Asks how to say or spell a word in Spanish
Names 15 classroom objects
commonErrors: EN: *¿Cómo se dice en español "pen"? word order is fine, but *¿Qué es "pen" en español? is less idiomatic
EN: does not recognise vosotros or ustedes plural imperatives used by teachers
boundaries: Imperative forms are taught in kt:es-imperative-affirmative; here they are recognised as fixed instructions
Repair phrases are kt:es-str-repair-basic

primitives.binding: Teacher instructions (abrid, subrayad, escribid en parejas) trigger actions on a virtual desk; action is the evidence
Learner collects classroom chunks from a recorded lesson into a personal phrase bank and uses one in the next task

kcs.label: Colours, size and everyday objects
kcs.description: Colour and size adjectives and personal objects: rojo, azul, verde, amarillo, blanco, negro, gris, marrón, naranja, rosa; grande, pequeño, largo, corto, nuevo, viejo; llaves, cartera, móvil, reloj, gafas. Naranja and rosa usually stay invariable (camisas naranja / naranjas both heard).
forms: grande / pequeño, largo / corto, nuevo / viejo
objects: las llaves, el móvil, el reloj, las gafas, la cartera

examples.es: Mi móvil es negro y pequeño.
examples.en: My mobile is black and small.

examples.es: ¿Dónde están mis gafas nuevas?
examples.en: Where are my new glasses?

mastery: Matches colour and size words to pictures
Describes five personal objects with colour and size
Finds the owner of lost objects by describing them in a role play
commonErrors: EN: forgets agreement with colour adjectives: *una casa blanco
EN: uses *café for brown in all varieties (marrón; café is common in parts of Latin America)
boundaries: Materials and shapes (de madera, redondo) are kt:es-describe-objects-a2
Agreement rules are kt:es-adjective-agreement

primitives.binding: Lost-property picture with coloured objects; learner describes one, partner identifies it; check colour, size and agreement
Object picture shown; learner types the noun with article and a colour before the answer appears

kcs.label: Cognates and false friends with English
kcs.description: Thousands of Spanish words share Latin roots with English and can be guessed (hospital, importante, información, -ción = -tion, -dad = -ty). Some look alike but differ in meaning (false friends): embarazada (pregnant), éxito (success), librería (bookshop), carpeta (folder), actual (current), sensible (sensitive), constipado (having a cold).
forms: false friends: embarazada, éxito, librería, carpeta, actual, sensible, constipado, asistir (attend)

examples.es: Estoy constipado: tengo frío y me duele la cabeza.
examples.en: I have a cold: I'm cold and my head hurts.

examples.es: La librería está al lado de la biblioteca.
examples.en: The bookshop is next to the library.

mastery: Guesses the meaning of 10 unseen cognates in a text
Spots and corrects false-friend errors in sentences
Uses context to decide whether a look-alike word is a true cognate
commonErrors: EN: *Estoy embarazada for "I'm embarrassed" (tengo vergüenza / me da vergüenza)
EN: reads librería as "library" (biblioteca)
EN: *actualmente used for "actually" (en realidad)
boundaries: Only general awareness; specific false friends are also listed in topic KCs
Spelling differences (ph → f, th → t) are noted, not drilled

primitives.binding: Learner writes the English-based guess for each look-alike, then compares with the real meaning and marks same / shifted / different
Short text with eight cognates and two false friends; learner guesses, then confirms or revises on a second encounter

citations.locator: Editorial (L1-specific); no framework locator
citations.note: PCIC inventories are written for all learners and do not address a particular first language. English-speaking learners can exploit thousands of Latin-based cognates and need warning about a small set of frequent false friends; the course is written for English speakers (instructionLang en).

kcs.label: Learning how to learn Spanish
kcs.description: Simple learning procedures for beginners: noting words with their article, grouping words by topic, using a bilingual dictionary, recording and listening to oneself, planning a task and checking it afterwards, managing anxiety about speaking, and working well in pairs.

examples.es: Siempre escribo las palabras con el artículo: el mapa, la mano.
examples.en: I always write words with the article: el mapa, la mano.

examples.es: Antes de hablar, preparo tres frases.
examples.en: Before speaking, I prepare three sentences.

mastery: Keeps a vocabulary list with gender marked for every noun

Plans, records and reviews a 30-second self-introduction
commonErrors: EN: lists nouns without gender, then guesses articles
EN: picks the first dictionary translation without checking word class
boundaries: General learning strategies; PCIC lists them without levels
Communication strategies in conversation are kt:es-str-repair-basic and kt:es-str-backchannel

primitives.binding: Learner looks up "match" for a given sentence in a bilingual dictionary page and must pick the right sense using labels
Record a 30-second introduction, compare with a model, note one thing to change, record again

kcs.label: Possessive determiners: mi, tu, su…
kcs.description: mi, tu, su, nuestro/a, vuestro/a, su go before the noun and agree with the thing owned, not the owner: mis libros, nuestra casa. Su/sus can mean his, her, its, their or your (usted/ustedes), so de + person is added when unclear.

examples.es: Mis padres viven en Lima y mi hermana vive en Quito.
examples.en: My parents live in Lima and my sister lives in Quito.

examples.es: ¿Es su coche, señora? – Sí, es mi coche.
examples.en: Is it your car, madam? – Yes, it's my car.

mastery: Chooses the possessive agreeing with the thing owned
Disambiguates su by rewriting with de + person
Presents their family photo using possessives
commonErrors: EN: agrees with the owner: *sus casa for "their house" (su casa)
EN: *nuestro casa (nuestro agrees in gender)
EN: uses possessive with body parts: *Me duele mi cabeza (see A2)
boundaries: Stressed possessives mío, tuyo are kt:es-possessives-stressed
de + owner is kt:es-de-possession

primitives.binding: Sentences where only the possessive shows one or many owners/things (su libro / sus libros / nuestros libros); learner picks the picture
Family photo: learner presents people and their things; check possessive agrees with the thing, not the owner

kcs.label: Possession and relation with de
kcs.description: Spanish has no 's: possession and many noun relations use de: el coche de mi padre, la clase de español, la vecina del tercero. de + el contracts to del. ¿De quién es? asks who owns something.
forms: noun + de + owner: la casa de Pablo
de + el = del: la puerta del hotel
noun + de + noun: una clase de inglés, un vaso de agua

examples.es: Es el perro de mis vecinos.
examples.en: It's my neighbours' dog.

examples.es: La profesora de español es de Bolivia.
examples.en: The Spanish teacher is from Bolivia.

mastery: Translates English 's phrases into de phrases
Uses del whenever de meets el
Says who owns objects in a lost-property game
commonErrors: EN: *Pablo casa or *la Pablo's casa
EN: *de el instead of del
EN: noun compounds in English order: *un español profesor for "a Spanish teacher" (un profesor de español)
boundaries: Possessive determiners are kt:es-possessives-unstressed
Other uses of de (origin, material) are in kt:es-prep-a-en-de and kt:es-describe-objects-a2

primitives.binding: Drag English-like pieces into Spanish order [cosa] de [dueño]; wrong order names the rule
Align "my brother's teacher's car" with "el coche del profesor de mi hermano" chunk by chunk

kcs.label: Family and relationships
kcs.description: Family words: padre, madre, padres (parents), hermano/a, hijo/a, abuelo/a, tío/a, primo/a, sobrino/a, nieto/a, marido/mujer, pareja, novio/a; A2 adds suegros, cuñado/a, hijo único, gemelos. Masculine plural covers mixed groups: los hermanos = brothers or brothers and sisters.
forms: masculine plural for mixed groups: mis hijos

examples.es: Tengo dos hermanos: un chico y una chica.
examples.en: I have two siblings: a boy and a girl.

examples.es: Mis abuelos tienen cinco nietos.
examples.en: My grandparents have five grandchildren.

mastery: Completes a family tree from a spoken description
Explains what los padres and los hermanos can refer to
Describes their own family in 5–6 sentences
commonErrors: EN: uses parientes for parents (padres; parientes = relatives)
EN: says *mis hermanos y hermanas when the mixed masculine plural is enough
boundaries: Family as a social concept (types of family) is sociocultural content flagged in kt:es-soc-greeting-customs and the topic KCs
Possessives are kt:es-possessives-unstressed

primitives.binding: Each partner has half a family tree and asks ¿Quién es…? ¿Cuántos hijos tiene…? to complete it
Family tree with blanks; learner types the relation word before it is revealed; first attempt kept

kcs.label: Describing appearance and character
kcs.description: Ser + adjective for build and character (alto, bajo, delgado, simpático, tímido), tener + noun for features (tiene el pelo rizado, los ojos azules), llevar for clothes, glasses and beards (lleva gafas). Antonym pairs help memory: alto/bajo, guapo/feo, simpático/antipático.
forms: tener el pelo largo/corto/rizado, los ojos verdes
A2: optimista, tranquilo, nervioso, generoso, amable

examples.es: Mi hermano es alto y delgado, tiene el pelo corto y lleva gafas.
examples.en: My brother is tall and thin, has short hair and wears glasses.

examples.es: Es un poco tímida, pero muy simpática.
examples.en: She's a bit shy but very nice.

mastery: Matches descriptions to people in a picture
Chooses ser, tener or llevar for each feature
Describes a famous person well enough for a partner to guess who
commonErrors: EN: *Es pelo largo / *Tiene alto (wrong verb)
EN: uses estar for permanent traits: *Está alto
EN: gordo used bluntly; Spanish speakers often soften with un poco or use alternatives
boundaries: estar + adjective for temporary states is kt:es-estar-states
Comparing people is kt:es-comparatives

primitives.binding: Group photo: learner describes one person; elements (pelo, gafas, altura, ropa) are checked against the picture
Feature cards: learner must choose ser / tener / llevar by meaning (alto, gafas, el pelo rizado, barba)

kcs.label: Joining ideas: y, o, pero, ni
kcs.description: y (and), o (or), pero (but) and ni (nor) join words and clauses. y becomes e before a word starting with the sound /i/ (español e inglés) and o becomes u before /o/ (siete u ocho). Ni appears with negatives: No como carne ni pescado.
forms: y / e (before i-, hi-): padre e hijo
o / u (before o-, ho-): uno u otro
pero: Es caro, pero es bonito.
ni: No tengo tiempo ni dinero.

examples.es: Hablo francés e inglés, pero no hablo alemán.
examples.en: I speak French and English, but I don't speak German.

examples.es: ¿Quieres té o café? – Ni té ni café, gracias.
examples.en: Do you want tea or coffee? – Neither tea nor coffee, thanks.

mastery: Chooses y/e and o/u correctly
Joins two short sentences with the right conjunction
Writes a short profile using y, pero and o at least once each
commonErrors: EN: *español y inglés (e is needed before i-)
EN: uses pero for "but rather" after negatives (sino, B1)
EN: double negation with ni avoided: *No tengo tiempo o dinero
boundaries: Connectors of cause and result are kt:es-porque-por-que and kt:es-por-eso-entonces
sino is B1

primitives.binding: Two short sentences to combine with y/pero/o; learner chooses the joiner by intended meaning and sees what is lost when split again
Rule y→e before /i/, o→u before /o/; apply to unseen pairs (agua y hielo, madre e hija, siete u ocho)

kcs.label: Present tense of regular -ar, -er, -ir verbs
kcs.description: Regular verbs drop -ar/-er/-ir and add person endings: hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, habláis, hablan; como, comes, come, comemos, coméis, comen; vivo, vives, vive, vivimos, vivís, viven. The present covers habits, facts, the moment now (Estamos en clase) and states that last (Vivo en Madrid).
forms: stress on the stem except nosotros/vosotros: TRAbajo, trabaJAmos
voseo forms (vos hablás, comés, vivís) recognised only

examples.es: Trabajo en una tienda y estudio por la noche.
examples.en: I work in a shop and study at night.

examples.es: ¿Dónde vivís? – Vivimos cerca del centro.
examples.en: Where do you (pl.) live? – We live near the centre.

mastery: Identifies person and number from regular endings
Conjugates unseen regular verbs in all persons
Describes their weekly routine with at least eight different regular verbs
commonErrors: EN: uses the infinitive: *Yo hablar español
EN: mixes -er and -ir endings in nosotros: *vivemos
EN: adds estar: *Estoy trabajo en un banco
EN: stresses the ending: *trabaJO for TRAbajo vs trabajÓ (past)
boundaries: Stem-changing and irregular-yo verbs are kt:es-present-stem-change and kt:es-present-irregular-yo
Progressive estar + gerund is kt:es-estar-gerund

primitives.binding: Learner derives the three ending sets, then conjugates unseen regular verbs (bailar, aprender, escribir); each step shows stem + ending
Sentences without subjects; learner must say who acts using only the verb ending

kcs.label: Negation and basic word order
kcs.term: la negación y el orden de palabras
kcs.description: Negate by putting no directly before the verb (and before object pronouns): No hablo francés. No lo sé. Answers often repeat no: ¿Eres francés? – No, no soy francés. Neutral order is subject–verb–object, but the subject can follow the verb or be dropped, and questions keep the same order.
forms: subject after verb is common: ¿Dónde vive Ana? / Llega el tren.

examples.es: ¿Eres de México? – No, no soy de México, soy de Guatemala.
examples.en: Are you from Mexico? – No, I'm not from Mexico, I'm from Guatemala.

examples.es: Marta no come carne.
examples.en: Marta doesn't eat meat.

mastery: Places no in the right position in sentences with and without pronouns
Corrects wrong statements with No, no…, … / Sí, sí…
Gives negative answers in a quick question-answer game
commonErrors: EN: puts no after the verb: *Hablo no francés
EN: invents an auxiliary: *No hago hablar
EN: single no in answers sounds abrupt to some speakers; No, no… is common
boundaries: Double negatives (no… nada/nunca/nadie) are kt:es-double-negation
Object pronoun placement with no is kt:es-clitic-position

primitives.binding: Drag no, pronoun and verb into slots; wrong placement names the rule "no directly before the (pronoun +) verb"
Quiz show with false statements about the learner; they must correct each with No, no…, … / Sí, sí…

kcs.label: Yes/no questions and tag questions
kcs.description: Yes/no questions keep the statement order and change only intonation (and ¿?): ¿Tienes hermanos? A tag ¿no? or ¿verdad? asks for confirmation: Eres Julián, ¿no? Alternatives use o: ¿Prefieres té o café?
forms: subject may move after the verb: ¿Vive aquí tu madre?
negative question asking for confirmation: ¿No conoces a Marta? (A2)

examples.es: Eres el hermano de Paula, ¿no? – Sí, soy yo.
examples.en: You're Paula's brother, right? – Yes, that's me.

examples.es: ¿Habla usted inglés?
examples.en: Do you speak English?

mastery: Turns statements into questions with correct punctuation and intonation
Uses ¿no? / ¿verdad? to check information
Conducts a find-someone-who survey with yes/no questions
commonErrors: EN: tries to translate "do": *¿Haces tú hablar…?
EN: uses ¿no? after negative statements, which can confuse; ¿verdad? is safer
boundaries: Intonation patterns are kt:es-phon-intonation; question words are kt:es-interrogatives-basic
Rhetorical and echo questions are kt:es-str-backchannel

primitives.binding: Find-someone-who grid: learner must ask yes/no questions to fill names; only questions with correct verb person get answers
Learner hears statement vs question versions and marks punctuation; then says both
